content: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder in which autoantibodies disrupt neuromuscular transmission, leading to muscle weakness. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) is hypothesized to be beneficial for this condition, as it is for other autoimmune diseases. This review aimed to evaluate the efficacy of IVIg in treating either acute exacerbations or chronic forms of myasthenia gravis. A total of seven randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified, each differing in inclusion criteria, comparator treatments, and outcome measures. In one trial involving 51 participants experiencing worsening myasthenia gravis, IVIg was compared to placebo. After 14 days, the quantitative myasthenia gravis score (QMGS) showed a mean difference (MD) of -1.60 (95% confidence interval [CI] -3.23 to 0.03), which was borderline statistically significant in favor of IVIg. In an unblinded study of 87 participants with exacerbations, IVIg was compared to plasma exchange. After 15 days, there was no significant difference in the myasthenic muscle score (MMS) between the two groups (MD -1.00; 95% CI -7.72 to 5.72). Similarly, in a study of 84 participants with worsening myasthenia gravis, no significant difference was observed in the change in QMGS 14 days after treatment with either IVIg or plasma exchange (MD -1.50; 95% CI -3.43 to 0.43). A smaller study involving 12 participants with moderate to severe myasthenia gravis, which had a high risk of bias due to skewed allocation, reported a significant reduction in QMGS for both IVIg and plasma exchange after four weeks (P < 0.05). Another study with 15 participants with mild to moderate myasthenia gravis found no significant difference in QMGS 42 days after treatment with IVIg or placebo (MD 1.60; 95% CI -1.92 to 5.12). In a trial of 33 participants with moderate exacerbations of myasthenia gravis, no significant difference was observed in QMGS 14 days after treatment with IVIg or methylprednisolone (MD -0.42; 95% CI -1.20 to 0.36). These smaller studies were underpowered to detect meaningful differences. The largest trial included 168 participants with exacerbations and compared two different doses of IVIg (2 g/kg versus 1 g/kg). No significant difference in MMS was observed after 15 days (MD 3.84; 95% CI -0.98 to 8.66). Adverse events associated with IVIg were generally mild and self-limiting, including fever, nausea, and headache. These side effects were subjectively reported to be less severe than those associated with plasma exchange, although no statistical comparison was possible based on the available data. Most trials were at low risk of bias, except where specific limitations were noted. In conclusion, one RCT provided some evidence supporting the efficacy of IVIg for exacerbations of myasthenia gravis, while two others found no significant difference between IVIg and plasma exchange. Another trial found no significant difference between 1 g/kg and 2 g/kg doses of IVIg. A further underpowered study showed no significant difference between IVIg and oral methylprednisolone. For chronic myasthenia gravis, there is insufficient evidence from RCTs to determine the efficacy of IVIg.
